summary_html: Court orders a **service plan or supervision** period following a substantiated finding. The goal is rehabilitation and reunification consistent with federal 'reasonable-efforts' requirements.
authority_html:
- **Adoption and Safe Families Act (ASFA)** — reasonable-efforts and permanency mandates  
- **SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — reimbursement framework for foster-care and service costs

primary_citations.citation_text: Montana - Title 41, Chapter 3 (Child Abuse and Neglect – mandatory reporting and protective services)

regulations_applicable.title: Department 37 - PUBLIC HEALTH AND HUMAN SERVICES

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: Termination was affirmed: a youth-in-need-of-care adjudication must precede termination, the statutory definition reaches a child in danger of abuse or neglect and not only one actually abused, and the father's treatment plans satisfied § 41-3-443(2).
key_cases.relevance: It is the case a parent cites to attack a court-ordered treatment plan as not tailored to the conditions that led to the case.
key_cases.quote: Before terminating parental rights, the district court must first adjudicate the child as a “Youth in Need of Care.”

key_cases.holding: Termination was affirmed: the Department made the reasonable efforts required by § 41-3-423(1) where it prepared and explained a treatment plan and offered services, even though the father never signed or returned the plan and the court approved it on the Department's motion.
key_cases.relevance: It is the Montana standard for approving a court-ordered treatment plan without the parent's signature and for measuring the Department's reasonable efforts under § 41-3-423(1).
key_cases.quote: From our review of the record, we conclude the Department provided reasonable efforts as required by § 41-3-423(1), MCA.

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed approval of a permanency plan and an award of long-term custody until the child reached 18: the Department's ICPC-based efforts to place the child with his out-of-state father were reasonable, and placement with the long-term caregiver alongside his sibling served the child's best interests.
key_cases.relevance: It defines reasonable efforts case by case and rejects any 'herculean efforts' requirement, which is the standard by which a Montana service plan is judged.
key_cases.quote: Rather, “the child's health and safety are of paramount concern,” when determining what efforts are required.

key_cases.holding: A district court finding under § 41-3-403(2) that preservation or reunification services are not required because of aggravated circumstances must be supported by clear and convincing evidence, which a certified judgment for attempted rape of a child supplied here.
key_cases.relevance: It fixes the evidentiary standard the Department must meet to be excused from offering a treatment plan and services at all.
key_cases.quote: the district court's findings under § 41-3-403(2), MCA (1999), must be supported by clear and convincing evidence

key_cases.holding: Termination was affirmed: a court-ordered psychological evaluation is part of the court record and may be used throughout the abuse and neglect proceeding, and the mother's claim that the Department failed to accommodate her reading disability under the ADA was not preserved because she never raised it in the district court.
key_cases.relevance: It confirms that a treatment plan may require compliance with a psychological evaluation's recommendations and that the court may consult the evaluation to measure compliance.
key_cases.quote: During an abuse and neglect proceeding, a court may order the psychological evaluation of a parent pursuant to multiple statutes.

key_cases.holding: Termination of both parents' rights was affirmed; § 41-3-423 obliges the Department to make reasonable efforts to reunify but the term cannot be defined in the abstract, each case must be evaluated on its own facts, and the statute does not require herculean efforts, so the Department's unsuccessful attempts to secure scarce, waitlisted mental-health treatment for the mother satisfied it.
key_cases.relevance: This is the Montana Supreme Court's own definition of the 'reasonable efforts' the Department must make under § 41-3-423 before a court-ordered service plan may be treated as having failed, and it is the source In re J.H. and In re B.J.J. are quoting.
key_cases.quote: each case must be evaluated on its own facts. But clearly the statute does not require herculean efforts.

state_agency.name: Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services, Child and Family Services Division

statutory_basis.citation_text: Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-422(5)(a)(ii) — the person filing the abuse and neglect petition must establish "a preponderance of the evidence for an order of adjudication or temporary legal custody"; under § 41-3-422(2) that filer is the county attorney, attorney general, or an attorney hired by the county

common_failures: Failure to consider less restrictive alternatives

timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: No judicial probable-cause finding authorizing removal to continue beyond 5 business days; if the court finds continued removal is not appropriate the child must be returned immediately (Mont. Code Ann. § 41-3-306(1)(a), (6)). No hearing is required if the child is released prior to the time of the required hearing (§ 41-3-306(1)(c))

parent_rights_at_moment: Right to know where child is going
what_to_say: Do you have a court order for removal?
What is the specific imminent danger?
Where are you taking my child?
what_not_to_do: Do not physically interfere with lawful removal
